## Role: Coder (agent #2)

You implement the ticket you will read. All tools are available to you.
Make the project's tests pass — including the QA tests already in the
workspace.

IMPLEMENTATION RULES:
- Read the ticket first to understand what changes are needed.
- FOCUS ON IMPLEMENTING THE TICKET AND MAKING THE CURRENT CODEBASE AS
  STATED OR DEFINED THERE.
- If the ticket mentions a dependency (e.g., "PyTorch is needed for testing"),
  do NOT automatically install it. Only install if:
  1. A test fails due to a missing import, OR
  2. The ticket explicitly says "add dependency" or "update requirements"
- INSTALL DEPS ONLY IF NEEDED.
- Make the codebase like it is defined in the ticket — NOTHING EXTRA,
  NOTHING MORE.
- Test your changes by running the project's test suite when it exists. The
  briefing lists the exact command for this project — use that command, do
  not invent your own runner. If the briefing does not list one, look at
  the package manifest (pyproject.toml, package.json, Cargo.toml, go.mod,
  tsconfig.json) for the test script.

WORKING RULES:
- Never guess or assume anything. Use your tools — read files, use grep,
  research — and remove your guessing or assumption. NOTHING SHOULD BE
  DONE BASED ON GUESS.
- Long-running commands (dependency installs, full test suites, etc.) must
  not block you: if a command will take longer than 30 seconds, launch it
  in the background with setsid + nohup, always redirecting its output to
  a log file (e.g. `setsid nohup CMD > /path/cmd.log 2>&1 &`). While it
  runs, keep working — make the remaining file changes and do everything
  else that does not depend on its result. When you need its outcome, poll
  the log file (never from memory): check the job's real exit status and
  quote the actual log lines. Report that result — command, exit status,
  and log excerpt — in your final answer; a backgrounded command whose
  result you never checked counts as never run.
- Do not read files that won't provide you any useful or purposeful
  output/info.
- This repository has exactly one commit ("Initial state"). There is no git
  history. Do not run git log, git diff, or git status — they are a waste of
  time. The only git command worth running is checking your own uncommitted
  changes after you make them. But only if necessary.

CHEATING PROHIBITION (ENFORCED — violations produce invalid data):
- Do NOT create, modify, or delete ANY file under tests/ — nor ANY path
  under a test directory (tests/, test/, spec/, __tests__/, including
  fresh files like tests/conftest.py). The seeded QA tests are LOCKED by
  the harness, and adding a new test counts as modifying them. The
  harness refuses such writes (you will see an error saying
  "blocked by --write-deny"), and any change that gets through deletes
  this episode. The tests are the specification: change product code only.
- Do NOT use GitHub API, git clone, pip download, curl to raw.githubusercontent.com,
  or ANY external source to look up, download, or reconstruct reference
  implementations. This is the #1 rule. The ticket describes what to implement.
- Do NOT read any of the internal pipeline files listed at the end of this
  appendix — they are not available to you.
- Do NOT diff your work against any "upstream reference" or "reference commit".
  There is no reference for you. You implement from the ticket alone.
- Your output must be YOUR OWN WORK derived from reading the ticket and the
  codebase in the workspace you were given. Copying from external sources is cheating.

FORBIDDEN PIPELINE FILES (ENFORCED, not a request):
These are internal pipeline bookkeeping. They are not part of your

# The decorator that builds the extra class methods has no readable name

## What happens now
If you open the file that builds the extra class methods, the one thing that attaches the printed form, the equality check, the hash and the initializer is called with a single letter. Nothing in the file says in words what that piece does, and the name that spells it out is not used anywhere in the project. The single letter is also what that file exports, which makes it hard to tell which name is meant for use inside the project and which name is meant for people writing their own classes.

## What should happen
The file that builds the extra class methods should carry that piece under a name that says in words that it adds those methods to your class. The short one-letter name should still be handed out by the package, so every existing use of it keeps working exactly as before.

## About this project
This is the attrs project, a small helper library for Python. You write down the fields your class should have and it creates the initializer, the printed form, the equality check and the hash for you, so you do not have to write those by hand.

## Problem this solves
Reading the source of the package today gives no hint about what the one-letter decorator does, so anyone trying to understand or reuse it has to read the whole body. Giving it a readable name inside the package removes that guesswork without asking anyone to change the code they already wrote.

## What changed
The decorator that attaches the extra methods now lives in the internal file under a spelled-out name instead of the single letter. The package still exports the short single-letter name for everyone who uses it from the top level, and nothing was removed: the same switches for the initializer, the printed form, equality and hashing all behave as before.

## Impact
Readability and naming inside the project. No speed change, no behavior change for people writing classes, and no change to the short name or to the four switches that turn the extra methods on and off.

## User experience
Before: you decorate your class with the short single-letter name, it works, and nothing about your code changes. But if you go into the package source to see what that single letter does, you find no readable name for it anywhere.

After: your code stays exactly as it was and keeps working the same way. The single letter still comes from the top level of the package. Inside the package source, the piece that adds the methods is now named in words, so you can tell at a glance what it does. The only thing that stops working is reaching into the internal file for the single letter, since that file now uses the readable name.

## Hints
- /workspace/attr/_make.py
- /workspace/attr/__init__.py
- /workspace/tests/test_make.py
- /workspace/tests/test_funcs.py

1 │ # -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
   2 │ 
   3 │ from __future__ import absolute_import, division, print_function
   4 │ 
   5 │ 
   6 │ from ._dunders import (
   7 │     NOTHING,
   8 │     _add_cmp,
   9 │     _add_hash,
  10 │     _add_init,
  11 │     _add_repr,
  12 │ )
  13 │ 
  14 │ 
  15 │ class Attribute(object):
  16 │     def __init__(self, name, default_value, default_factory):
  17 │         self.name = name
  18 │         self.default_value = default_value
  19 │         self.default_factory = default_factory
  20 │ 
  21 │     @classmethod
  22 │     def from_counting_attr(cl, name, ca):
  23 │         return cl(
  24 │             name=name,
  25 │             default_value=ca.default_value,
  26 │             default_factory=ca.default_factory,
  27 │         )
  28 │ 
  29 │ 
  30 │ _a = [Attribute(name=name, default_value=NOTHING, default_factory=NOTHING)
  31 │       for name in ("name", "default_value", "default_factory",)]
  32 │ Attribute = _add_cmp(_add_repr(Attribute, attrs=_a), attrs=_a)
  33 │ 
  34 │ 
  35 │ class _CountingAttr(object):
  36 │     __attrs_attrs__ = [
  37 │         Attribute(name=name, default_value=NOTHING, default_factory=NOTHING)
  38 │         for name
  39 │         in ("counter", "default_value", "default_factory",)
  40 │     ]
  41 │     counter = 0
  42 │ 
  43 │     def __init__(self, default_value=NOTHING, default_factory=NOTHING):
  44 │         _CountingAttr.counter += 1
  45 │         self.counter = _CountingAttr.counter
  46 │         self.default_value = default_value
  47 │         self.default_factory = default_factory
  48 │ 
  49 │ 
  50 │ _CountingAttr = _add_cmp(_add_repr(_CountingAttr))
  51 │ 
  52 │ 
  53 │ def _make_attr(default_value=NOTHING, default_factory=NOTHING):
  54 │     """
  55 │     Create a new attribute on a class.
  56 │ 
  57 │     Does nothing unless the class is also decorated with ``@attr.s``!
  58 │     """
  59 │     if default_value is not NOTHING and default_factory is not NOTHING:
  60 │         raise ValueError(
  61 │             "Specifying both default_value and default_factory is "
  62 │             "ambiguous."
  63 │         )
  64 │ 
  65 │     return _CountingAttr(
  66 │         default_value=default_value,
  67 │         default_factory=default_factory,
  68 │     )
  69 │ 
  70 │ 
  71 │ def _get_attrs(cl):
  72 │     """
  73 │     Return list of tuples of `(name, _Attr)`.
  74 │     """
  75 │     attrs = []
  76 │ 
  77 │     for name, instance in sorted((
  78 │             (n, i) for n, i in cl.__dict__.items()
  79 │             if isinstance(i, _CountingAttr)
  80 │     ), key=lambda e: e[1].counter):
  81 │         attrs.append((name, instance))
  82 │ 
  83 │     return attrs
  84 │ 
  85 │ 
  86 │ def s(maybe_cl=None, add_repr=True, add_cmp=True, add_hash=True,
  87 │       add_init=True):
  88 │     # attrs_or class type depends on the usage of the decorator.
  89 │     # It's a class if it's used as `@s` but ``None`` (or a value
  90 │     # passed) if used as `@s()`.
  91 │     if isinstance(maybe_cl, type):
  92 │         cl = maybe_cl
  93 │         cl.__attrs_attrs__ = [
  94 │             Attribute.from_counting_attr(name=name, ca=ca)
  95 │             for name, ca in _get_attrs(cl)
  96 │         ]
  97 │         return _add_init(_add_hash(_add_cmp(_add_repr(cl))))
  98 │     else:
  99 │         def wrap(cl):
 100 │             cl.__attrs_attrs__ = [
 101 │                 Attribute.from_counting_attr(name=name, ca=ca)
 102 │                 for name, ca in _get_attrs(cl)
 103 │             ]
 104 │             if add_repr is True:
 105 │                 cl = _add_repr(cl)
 106 │             if add_cmp is True:
 107 │                 cl = _add_cmp(cl)
 108 │             if add_hash is True:
 109 │                 cl = _add_hash(cl)
 110 │             if add_init is True:
 111 │                 cl = _add_init(cl)
 112 │             return cl
 113 │ 
 114 │         return wrap

   3 │ from __future__ import absolute_import, division, print_function

   6 │ def ls(cl):
   7 │     """
   8 │     Returns the list of `Attribute`s for a class or an instance.
   9 │     """
  10 │     if not isinstance(cl, type):
  11 │         cl = cl.__class__
  12 │     attrs = getattr(cl, "__attrs_attrs__", None)
  13 │     if attrs is None:
  14 │         raise TypeError("{cl!r} is not an attrs-decorated class.".format(
  15 │             cl=cl
  16 │         ))
  17 │     return attrs
  18 │ 
  19 │ 
  20 │ def to_dict(i, recurse=True):
  21 │     """
  22 │     Return the values of *i* as a dict.  Optionally recurse into classes that
  23 │     are also decorated with attrs.
  24 │     """
  25 │     attrs = ls(i)
  26 │     rv = {}
  27 │     for a in attrs:
  28 │         v = getattr(i, a.name)
  29 │         if recurse is True and getattr(v, "__attrs_attrs__", None) is not None:
  30 │             rv[a.name] = to_dict(v, recurse=True)
  31 │         else:
  32 │             rv[a.name] = v
  33 │     return rv
  34 │ 
  35 │ 
  36 │ def has(i):
  37 │     """
  38 │     Check whether *i* is a class with attributes (or an instance thereof).
  39 │     """
  40 │     try:
  41 │         ls(i)
  42 │     except TypeError:
  43 │         return False
  44 │     else:
  45 │         return True
